quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — What AI Actually Is
quizzes.intro: Check whether you can separate real AI concepts from hype before going deeper into learning systems.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes artificial intelligence?

options.text: Software that is conscious and understands the world like a human
A family of techniques that let computers perform tasks associated with intelligent behavior
Any program that runs automatically on a schedule
A single algorithm that solves every problem

questions.explanation: AI is defined by capability, not consciousness. It covers systems that recognize patterns, predict, classify, generate, plan, or adapt.

wrongExplanations.a: Current AI systems do not have human-like consciousness or understanding, even when outputs look fluent.
wrongExplanations.c: Automation can be simple rule-based scheduling; that alone is not AI.
wrongExplanations.d: AI is a broad field with many methods, not one universal algorithm.

questions.prompt: What is the best relationship between AI, machine learning, and deep learning?

options.text: They are three unrelated fields
Deep learning contains AI, and AI contains machine learning
AI is broadest; machine learning is one approach; deep learning is a subset of machine learning
Machine learning is always generative AI

questions.explanation: AI is the broad field. Machine learning learns from data. Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks within machine learning.

wrongExplanations.a: They are nested related concepts, not unrelated fields.
wrongExplanations.b: That nesting is reversed: AI contains ML, and ML contains deep learning.
wrongExplanations.d: Machine learning includes many non-generative tasks like classification, ranking, and forecasting.

questions.prompt: Why does training data quality matter so much?

options.text: Because models ignore data after deployment
Because models learn patterns from examples, so biased or incomplete data shapes biased or weak behavior
Because more rows always guarantee perfect accuracy
Because AI systems invent correct labels automatically

questions.explanation: A model’s experience is its data. Poor, biased, leaked, or incomplete examples produce poor, biased, or misleading behavior.

wrongExplanations.a: Deployed models still reflect what they learned from training data.
wrongExplanations.c: Volume helps only when data is relevant, representative, and correctly labeled.
wrongExplanations.d: Labels and examples usually come from humans, sensors, or prior systems—not automatic perfect truth.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet formula that always multiplies price by 1.18 is best described as:

options.text: Deep learning
Generative AI
Traditional automation / fixed rules
Unsupervised clustering

questions.explanation: Fixed formulas follow explicit rules. They are useful automation, but they are not learning systems.

wrongExplanations.a: Deep learning learns patterns from data using neural networks.
wrongExplanations.b: Generative AI creates new content such as text or images.
wrongExplanations.d: Clustering groups similar items; it does not apply a fixed tax multiplier.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a model to generalize?

options.text: It memorizes every training example exactly
It performs well on new examples it has not seen before
It only works on the original training file
It refuses to make predictions

questions.explanation: Generalization is the ability to apply learned patterns to fresh cases, which is the real goal of training.

wrongExplanations.a: Exact memorization is overfitting, not robust learning.
wrongExplanations.c: That would mean the model failed to transfer beyond training examples.
wrongExplanations.d: Prediction on new cases is usually the point of a deployed model.

questions.prompt: Which question best tests whether a product truly uses machine learning?

options.text: Does the marketing page say “AI-powered”?
Does the system learn patterns from data and improve predictions from examples rather than only fixed rules?
Does it run in the cloud?
Does it have a chatbot window?

questions.explanation: Machine learning is about learning from data. Branding, hosting location, and chat UI alone do not define ML.

wrongExplanations.a: Marketing labels are not technical evidence.
wrongExplanations.c: Cloud hosting is an infrastructure choice, not a learning method.
wrongExplanations.d: A chatbot can be rule-based, retrieval-based, generative, or a hybrid—UI alone proves little.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Tasks, Case Studies, and Limits
quizzes.intro: Apply AI task vocabulary and judge where systems are strong, weak, or risky.

questions.prompt: Predicting next month’s sales number is mainly which task type?

options.text: Classification
Regression
Clustering
Image generation

questions.explanation: Regression predicts continuous numeric values such as sales, temperature, or delivery time.

wrongExplanations.a: Classification predicts categories/labels, not continuous amounts.
wrongExplanations.c: Clustering groups similar items without predicting a sales number.
wrongExplanations.d: Image generation creates pictures; it is not a sales forecast.

questions.prompt: Which example is generative AI?

options.text: A filter that sorts emails into folders using fixed keywords
A tool that drafts a product description from a short brief
A thermostat set to 21°C
A calculator computing tax

questions.explanation: Generative AI creates new content. Drafting product copy is a classic generation task.

wrongExplanations.a: Fixed keyword rules are traditional automation.
wrongExplanations.c: A fixed temperature setting is not generative.
wrongExplanations.d: A calculator applies arithmetic rules.

questions.prompt: Which is a core limitation of current language models?

options.text: They never produce fluent text
Fluency can hide false or outdated information
They cannot be used for drafting
They always cite perfect sources

questions.explanation: Models can sound confident while being wrong. Fluency is not the same as truth.

wrongExplanations.a: Modern language models are often highly fluent.
wrongExplanations.c: Drafting is one of their strongest practical uses when verified.
wrongExplanations.d: They do not reliably provide perfect citations.

questions.prompt: A medical imaging model should usually be treated as:

options.text: A full replacement for clinicians
A decision-support tool that still needs expert judgment
Proof that AI has human understanding
A system that cannot make false negatives

questions.explanation: In high-stakes domains, AI can assist review and prioritization, but accountability and clinical judgment remain human.

wrongExplanations.a: Replacement is unsafe and usually not appropriate.
wrongExplanations.c: Useful performance does not equal human understanding.
wrongExplanations.d: Any model can miss cases; monitoring false negatives is critical.

questions.prompt: Which question is most useful before adopting an AI tool?

options.text: Does the demo look impressive for 30 seconds?
What data was it trained on, what is it optimized for, and how are errors handled?
Does the vendor use the word revolutionary?
Can it replace every employee immediately?

questions.explanation: Serious adoption depends on data, task fit, evaluation, and failure handling—not marketing language.

wrongExplanations.a: Short demos hide edge cases and failure modes.
wrongExplanations.d: Immediate total replacement is rarely realistic or safe.

questions.prompt: In a fraud detection system, why are thresholds and review workflows so important?

options.text: Because fraud models never make mistakes
Because false declines and missed fraud have different costs, so score bands need human process design
Because thresholds remove the need for monitoring
Because all transactions should be blocked by default forever

questions.explanation: Fraud decisions are asymmetric: blocking good customers and missing real fraud both hurt. Thresholds map scores into actions with oversight.

wrongExplanations.a: Fraud models make errors and face adaptive attackers.
wrongExplanations.c: Monitoring remains essential as behavior and attacks change.
wrongExplanations.d: Blocking everything would destroy legitimate commerce.

questions.prompt: A course recommender that only maximizes clicks may still be a poor learning product because:

options.text: Clicks are illegal to measure
Engagement metrics can diverge from mastery, sequencing quality, and long-term learner goals
Recommenders cannot use user history
Students never click useful courses

questions.explanation: Objective functions encode values. Click maximization can promote addictive or mismatched content instead of effective learning paths.

wrongExplanations.a: Clicks are commonly measured; legality is not the core issue here.
wrongExplanations.c: User history is a standard recommender signal.
wrongExplanations.d: Students do click useful courses; the issue is metric misalignment.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — AI Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use everything from the lesson. Focus on decisions, governance, and failure modes—not buzzwords.

questions.prompt: A company wants AI to “improve the business” with no clearer goal. What should happen first?

options.text: Buy the most expensive model available
Define a specific task, data sources, success metrics, and error costs
Replace the whole analytics team
Skip measurement because AI is inherently valuable

questions.explanation: Vague goals produce vague projects. Useful AI starts with a clear task and evaluation plan.

wrongExplanations.a: Cost does not define fitness for the problem.
wrongExplanations.c: Replacement without a defined task is reckless.
wrongExplanations.d: Without measurement you cannot know if the system helps.

questions.prompt: Which scenario most needs stronger safeguards?

options.text: Movie recommendations
Playlist sorting
Loan approval scoring
Emoji suggestion

questions.explanation: Loan decisions affect people’s finances and fairness. High-stakes domains need auditability, monitoring, and human accountability.

wrongExplanations.a: Wrong movie picks are low-cost errors.
wrongExplanations.b: Playlist mistakes are inconvenient, not high-stakes.
wrongExplanations.d: Emoji suggestions have tiny consequences.

questions.prompt: If a hiring model is trained on ten years of biased past decisions, the most likely risk is:

options.text: The model becomes perfectly fair automatically
The model may learn and scale historical bias
Bias disappears because computers are neutral
The model cannot use historical data at all

questions.explanation: Models learn from examples. Biased history can become encoded behavior unless actively audited and corrected.

wrongExplanations.a: Fairness is not automatic.
wrongExplanations.c: Computers inherit the structure of their training data and labels.
wrongExplanations.d: Historical data can be used, but must be handled carefully.

questions.prompt: A chatbot answers customer questions fluently but often invents policy details. What is the best immediate response?

options.text: Trust fluency as proof of accuracy
Constrain answers with approved sources, add escalation, and measure factual errors
Remove all human support agents immediately
Increase temperature so answers sound more creative

questions.explanation: Grounding, escalation paths, and error measurement turn a risky chatbot into a controlled support tool.

wrongExplanations.a: Fluency can conceal hallucinations.
wrongExplanations.c: Removing humans increases risk when accuracy is weak.
wrongExplanations.d: More creativity usually worsens factual reliability.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows mature AI thinking?

options.text: AI is magic, so evaluation is unnecessary
AI is useless because it is not human
AI is a powerful tool whose value depends on task fit, data, metrics, and human oversight
If a vendor demo works once, production success is guaranteed

questions.explanation: Mature judgment treats AI as a tool: useful when fit is good, dangerous when evaluation and oversight are missing.

wrongExplanations.a: Magic thinking skips accountability.
wrongExplanations.b: Non-human methods can still be highly useful.
wrongExplanations.d: Demos are not production proof.

questions.prompt: Why can an accurate model still fail in a real workflow?

options.text: Because accuracy numbers are the only thing that matters
Because poor UX, alert fatigue, or misaligned incentives can stop people from using it well
Because models never need monitoring
Because users always follow model output perfectly

questions.explanation: AI lives inside products and organizations. Workflow fit and human factors determine real outcomes.

wrongExplanations.a: Offline accuracy is necessary but not sufficient.
wrongExplanations.d: Users may ignore, overtrust, or misuse outputs.

questions.prompt: Which checklist item is most important when deciding NOT to use machine learning yet?

options.text: The team dislikes dashboards
A transparent rule already solves the problem, or outcome data/labels and monitoring capacity are missing
Competitors use the word AI in ads
The dataset has more than one column

questions.explanation: Choosing not to use ML is mature when simpler methods work or when data and maintenance readiness are insufficient.

wrongExplanations.a: Dashboard preference is unrelated to ML readiness.
wrongExplanations.c: Competitor marketing should not drive architecture.
wrongExplanations.d: Having columns does not mean you have a solvable labeled learning problem.
